title: OSINT: The Intelligence That Was Always Public
content:
Before we go further, there is a term you need to understand precisely, because you will see it constantly in professional security:

OSINT.

Open Source Intelligence.

First: what 'open source' does NOT mean here. It does not mean open-source software. It does not mean Linux or Python or GitHub. 'Open source' in the intelligence world means publicly available. Accessible to anyone. No hacking required, no credentials needed, no legal risk. If a search engine can find it, if a government database lists it, if a company published it themselves — it is open source.

OSINT is intelligence gathered from public sources.

Here is the insight that surprises almost every beginner:

The amount of genuinely useful security intelligence available in public sources — about any real organisation — is enormous. And most organisations have no idea how much they are giving away.

**Where OSINT comes from**

Organisations create their own OSINT continuously, through normal business activity:

*Job postings* are one of the richest OSINT sources available. A single job listing can tell a professional attacker:
— The exact software stack in use ('Experience with Splunk, CrowdStrike Falcon, and Palo Alto Networks firewalls')
— Which cloud provider they use ('AWS or Azure experience required')
— Internal team structures ('You will report to the Head of Platform Engineering')
— What security gaps they are currently trying to fill ('Help us build our incident response capability from scratch')

Organisations post these publicly because they need to hire. They never consider that this is also an intelligence briefing for anyone planning an attack.

*LinkedIn profiles* reveal employee names, job titles, team hierarchies, internal project names (sometimes), and the technical skills employees list to attract recruiters. A complete picture of a company's IT and security team — who they are, what they know, who they report to — is often fully visible on LinkedIn.

*Press releases and news articles* announce technology partnerships, new software deployments, major contract wins, and infrastructure changes. 'Meridian Financial today announced a strategic partnership with Salesforce' tells an attacker which CRM platform Meridian uses and potentially which Salesforce-connected systems they have.

*SSL certificate logs* are public by design. Every time an organisation gets an SSL/TLS certificate for a domain (which happens for every website and many internal services), the certificate is logged in a public Certificate Transparency log. Tools like crt.sh let anyone search these logs — revealing subdomains, internal services, and staging environments that were never advertised publicly.

*Domain registration records (WHOIS)* show who registered a domain, when, which registrar they used, and often which name servers handle their DNS. Some organisations redact this information using privacy protection, but many do not.

*GitHub repositories* sometimes contain far more than intended. Developers occasionally commit configuration files with real database connection strings, API keys, or internal server names. Even when the credential itself has been rotated, the repository reveals internal naming conventions, server locations, and the technologies in use.

*Breach databases* record the organisations whose employee data has appeared in previous breaches. If a company's email domain appears in the Collection #1 data leak or a similar breach, attackers know that real, valid email addresses from that domain are in the dataset — and if any employees reused those passwords on corporate accounts, the door may already be open.

*Shodan* is a search engine that indexes publicly accessible internet-connected devices — web servers, databases, IoT devices, industrial control systems, network routers, and anything else that responds to a connection on the public internet. An organisation's public-facing infrastructure is often discoverable on Shodan before a penetration tester has sent a single packet.

**What a professional assembles from OSINT**

A skilled OSINT investigator working on a professional engagement builds what is called a target dossier — a structured intelligence document covering:

— The organisation's full technology stack (from job postings, LinkedIn profiles, press releases)
— Every confirmed employee in the IT and security department (from LinkedIn)
— Email naming format (confirmed from public sources, often a conference speaker page or news article)
— All known subdomains (from certificate transparency logs)
— Historical breach exposure (from HaveIBeenPwned and breach databases)
— Public-facing infrastructure overview (from Shodan and WHOIS)
— Any third-party vendors or partners with likely network access (from press releases, job postings, supply chain announcements)

This document is assembled entirely from public sources. It is completed before a single packet is sent to the target. And it shapes every decision made in the scanning and exploitation phases that follow.

**Why professionals use OSINT**

The question a new student often asks is: 'If I'm going to hack them anyway (with authorisation), why not just run tools and skip the research?'

Because reconnaissance determines precision. Active tools — Nmap, vulnerability scanners, web application fuzzers — generate a lot of data. But data without context is noise. OSINT converts noise into intelligence. It tells you which system to scan first, which vulnerability to check, which employee's account is most likely to be compromised, and which third-party partner is the softest entry point.

A penetration tester who skips OSINT spends two weeks scanning everything and misses the legacy.meridian-financial.com subdomain running software from 2014 — the one that Maya found in the certificate transparency log on day one.

callouts.title: Key OSINT Sources — Professional Reference
callouts.text:
WHOIS / who.is — domain registration records
crt.sh — SSL certificate transparency logs (subdomain discovery)
LinkedIn — employee enumeration and technology stack
Shodan.io — internet-connected device search engine
HaveIBeenPwned.com — breach database exposure check
archive.org / Wayback Machine — historical website snapshots
GitHub / GitLab — repository searches for leaked credentials
Job posting aggregators (Indeed, LinkedIn Jobs) — technology stack and team structure
Google Dorking — advanced search operators to find sensitive public files

callouts.title: Where This Appears in Certifications
callouts.text: OSINT and passive reconnaissance methodology is tested in CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) Domain 2: Footprinting and Reconnaissance, which accounts for 15% of the CEH exam. It also appears in the eJPT (eLearnSecurity Junior Penetration Tester) practical exam as the opening phase of every assessment. In a real OSCP engagement, examiners expect the report to show a structured reconnaissance phase before any scanning begins.

keyTerms.definition: Open Source Intelligence. Intelligence gathered from publicly available sources — websites, social media, public records, news archives, SSL certificate logs, WHOIS databases, and breach databases. Completely passive by definition: all sources are already public. No special access or tools are required, and no contact with the target is made.

A structured document built during the OSINT phase of a penetration test, compiling all discovered intelligence about the target: technology stack, employee directory, email format, known subdomains, historical breach exposure, public-facing infrastructure, and identified vendor relationships. Completed before any active scanning begins.

The use of advanced Google search operators to find specific information that Google has indexed but is not prominently displayed. Examples: site:company.com filetype:pdf to find all publicly indexed PDFs on a domain; inurl:admin to find admin panels; intitle:"index of" to find directory listings. Passive: you are using Google's public index, not contacting the target directly.

A public log of every SSL/TLS certificate issued by Certificate Authorities, required by browser security policy. Because certificates must be logged publicly, every subdomain that has ever received an HTTPS certificate is discoverable. Tools like crt.sh make this searchable. A critical passive reconnaissance source for subdomain discovery.
